note: Worked examples for example-first practice. Each has 3-6 short steps; 'turn' names the similar problem the student tries next.

examples.problem: A force $\mathbf F=(3\text{ N})\,\hat{\mathbf x}+(4\text{ N})\,\hat{\mathbf y}$ acts on a block. Find the component of $\mathbf F$ along a unit vector $\hat{\mathbf u}$ that points $30^\circ$ above the $+x$ axis.

steps.do: Write the unit vector in Cartesian components
steps.why: You can only project with the dot product once $\hat{\mathbf u}$ is written in components and has length 1.

steps.do: Project F onto û with the dot product
steps.why: The component along a unit vector is $\mathbf F\cdot\hat{\mathbf u}$. Multiply matching components and add.

steps.do: Plug in the numbers
steps.why: $\phi$ is measured from $+x$, so $\cos\phi$ goes with $F_x$ and $\sin\phi$ goes with $F_y$.

steps.do: Check using the magnitude and the angle between them
steps.why: $F_u=F\cos(\theta-\phi)$ must give the same result.

examples.takeaway: To get the component along a direction, write that direction as a unit vector $\hat{\mathbf u}=(\cos\phi,\sin\phi)$ and take $\mathbf F\cdot\hat{\mathbf u}$.
examples.review: Opus 5.5 wrote it from the confirmed note; Fable 5.1 solved it blind and checked the steps; code recomputed the answer (2026-09-23)

examples.problem: A block $M_1=2$ kg sits on a plane inclined at $\theta=30^\circ$ with kinetic friction coefficient $\mu=0.2$. A massless string over a massless pulley connects it to a hanging mass $M_2=3$ kg, and $M_1$ moves up the plane. Find the acceleration $a$.

steps.do: Write F = ma for the hanging mass
steps.why: Take down as positive for $M_2$. Gravity pulls it down and the tension pulls it up.

steps.do: Write F = ma along the incline for M1
steps.why: $N=M_1g\cos\theta$. $M_1$ moves up the plane, so friction $\mu N$ points down the plane.

steps.do: Add the equations to eliminate T
steps.why: The string gives both masses the same $a$, so adding the equations cancels the unknown $T$.

steps.do: Plug in the numbers
steps.why: $M_1\sin\theta=1$ kg and $\mu M_1\cos\theta=0.346$ kg.

examples.takeaway: Write $F=ma$ for each body along its own direction of motion, then add the equations so the tension cancels.
examples.review: Opus 5.5 wrote it from the confirmed note; Fable 5.1 solved it blind and checked the steps; code recomputed the answer (2026-09-23)

examples.problem: A 40 kg sled carrying you slides at 5 m/s along straight frictionless tracks. Then 10 kg of snow falls vertically onto it and comes to rest on the sled. What is the sled's final speed?

steps.do: List the external forces and pick the conserved direction
steps.why: Gravity and the track's normal forces have no component along the track, so $P$ along the track is conserved.

steps.do: Find the initial momentum along the track
steps.why: The snow falls vertically, so it has no momentum along the track.

steps.do: Find the final momentum of sled plus snow
steps.why: The snow ends up at rest on the sled, so both move together at $v$.

steps.do: Set P_i = P_f and solve for v
steps.why: Momentum along the track is conserved. Kinetic energy is not, because the snow sticks.

examples.takeaway: Conserve only the momentum component along which the external force is zero, and include every piece of the system.
examples.review: Opus 5.5 wrote it from the confirmed note; Fable 5.1 solved it blind and checked the steps; code recomputed the answer (2026-09-23)

examples.problem: A 2 kg mass moving at 3 m/s approaches a stationary 4 kg mass along a line. Find the kinetic energy in the CM frame, $K_{CM}$, which is the part of the lab kinetic energy not tied to the motion of the CM.

steps.do: Find the total mass and the CM velocity
steps.why: The CM frame moves at $u=\sum m_iv_i/M$, a mass-weighted average, not a plain one.

steps.do: Find the lab kinetic energy
steps.why: Only the 2 kg mass moves in the lab frame.

steps.do: Subtract the kinetic energy of the CM motion
steps.why: $K_S=K_{CM}+\tfrac12Mu^2$, because the cross term vanishes in the CM frame.

steps.do: Check with velocities in the CM frame
steps.why: $v_i'=v_i-u$. Check that $\sum m_iv_i'=4-4=0$.

examples.takeaway: Split the kinetic energy as $K_S=K_{CM}+\tfrac12Mu^2$ with $u=P/M$. The energy relative to the CM is what remains.
examples.review: Opus 5.5 wrote it from the confirmed note; Fable 5.1 solved it blind and checked the steps; code recomputed the answer (2026-09-23)

examples.problem: A pendulum bob sits at horizontal position $x=\ell\sin\theta$ with $\ell=2$ m. At some instant $\theta=0.5$ rad, $\dot\theta=3$ rad/s and $\ddot\theta=1$ rad/s$^2$. Find $\ddot x$.

steps.do: Differentiate once with the chain rule
steps.why: $\theta$ depends on $t$, so the derivative of the outer function picks up a factor of $\dot\theta$.

steps.do: Differentiate the product cosθ·θ̇
steps.why: Both factors depend on time. Differentiating $\cos\theta$ gives $-\sin\theta\,\dot\theta$, which produces the $\dot\theta^2$ term.

steps.do: Plug in the numbers
steps.why: $\cos0.5=0.8776$ and $\sin0.5=0.4794$. Remember to square $\dot\theta$.

steps.do: Simplify and check the sign
steps.why: The centripetal $\dot\theta^2$ term dominates and points back toward the axis, so $\ddot x<0$.

examples.takeaway: Treat $\dot f=f'(\theta)\dot\theta$ as a product, so $\ddot f=f''\dot\theta^2+f'\ddot\theta$. Never drop the $\dot\theta^2$ term.
examples.review: Opus 5.5 wrote it from the confirmed note; Fable 5.1 solved it blind and checked the steps; code recomputed the answer (2026-09-23)

examples.problem: A spring pendulum has $m=0.5$ kg, $k=20$ N/m and $\ell=1.0$ m. At one instant the stretch is $x=0.1$ m, $\theta=0.3$ rad and $\dot\theta=2$ rad/s. Take $g=9.8$ m/s². Find $\ddot x$ at that instant.

steps.do: Write T with radial and tangential parts
steps.why: The velocity has a radial part $\dot x$ and a tangential part $(\ell+x)\dot\theta$.

steps.do: Write V from gravity plus the spring
steps.why: The mass sits $(\ell+x)\cos\theta$ below the pivot, and the spring is stretched by $x$.

steps.do: Form L = T − V
steps.why: Use the minus sign. $T+V$ would be the energy, not the Lagrangian.

steps.do: Apply the E–L equation for x
steps.why: $\partial L/\partial\dot x=m\dot x$. Get $\partial L/\partial x$ by treating $\dot x$ and $\dot\theta$ as independent of $x$.

steps.do: Plug in the numbers
steps.why: The three terms are centripetal $4.4$, gravity $9.36$ and spring $-4$.

examples.takeaway: Write the scalars $T$ and $V$ in the natural coordinates, form $L=T-V$, and apply the E–L equation once for each coordinate.
examples.review: Opus 5.5 wrote it from the confirmed note; Fable 5.1 solved it blind and checked the steps; code recomputed the answer (2026-09-23)

examples.problem: A particle of mass $m=2$ kg moves in a plane under a central potential $V(r)$. At $r_1=1$ m it has $\dot\theta_1=4$ rad/s. Find $\dot\theta_2$ when it reaches $r_2=2$ m.

steps.do: Write L in polar coordinates
steps.why: Polar coordinates match the symmetry of $V(r)$.

steps.do: Check which coordinate is missing from L
steps.why: $\theta$ does not appear in $L$ (only $\dot\theta$ does), so $\theta$ is cyclic.

steps.do: Compute the conserved generalized momentum
steps.why: The E–L equation becomes $\frac{d}{dt}p_\theta=0$.

steps.do: Fix the constant from the initial data
steps.why: $p_\theta$ is constant, so its initial value holds at every later time.

steps.do: Solve for the angular speed at r₂
steps.why: $p_\theta$ is conserved, not $\dot\theta$. Doubling $r$ cuts $\dot\theta$ by a factor of four.

examples.takeaway: If $q$ is missing from $L$, then $\partial L/\partial\dot q$ (not $\dot q$) is a constant you can use right away.
examples.review: Opus 5.5 wrote it from the confirmed note; Fable 5.1 solved it blind and checked the steps; code recomputed the answer (2026-09-23)

examples.problem: A force $\mathbf F=(3,1,0)$ N acts at position $\mathbf r=(1,2,0)$ m. Find the $z$ component of the torque $\boldsymbol\tau=\mathbf r\times\mathbf F$.

steps.do: Write both vectors in components
steps.why: Keep the order $\mathbf r$ first, then $\mathbf F$. Swapping them flips the sign.

steps.do: Note that the x and y components vanish
steps.why: Both vectors lie in the $xy$-plane, so only $\tau_z$ survives.

steps.do: Apply the z-component formula
steps.why: The $z$ component uses the $x$ and $y$ labels in cyclic order.

steps.do: Evaluate and read off the sense
steps.why: A negative sign means clockwise seen from $+z$. The right-hand rule gives the same sense.

examples.takeaway: $(\mathbf a\times\mathbf b)_z=a_xb_y-a_yb_x$. Get the other components by cycling $x\to y\to z$, and keep the order.
examples.review: Opus 5.5 wrote it from the confirmed note; Fable 5.1 solved it blind and checked the steps; code recomputed the answer (2026-09-23)

examples.problem: A particle of mass $2$ kg is at $(x,y)=(3,1)$ m with velocity $(v_x,v_y)=(0.5,4)$ m/s, in the plane $z=0$. Find $L_z$ about the origin.

steps.do: Write r and v from the origin
steps.why: $\mathbf L$ depends on the origin, so measure $\mathbf r$ from the chosen point.

steps.do: Keep only L_z for planar motion
steps.why: $\mathbf r$ and $\mathbf v$ both lie in the $xy$-plane, so $\mathbf r\times\mathbf v$ points along $\hat{\mathbf z}$.

steps.do: Use the z-component formula
steps.why: This is $m(\mathbf r\times\mathbf v)_z$, with $\mathbf r$ first.

steps.do: Plug in the numbers
steps.why: A positive result means counterclockwise motion about the origin, seen from $+z$.

examples.takeaway: For planar motion, $L_z=m(xv_y-yv_x)$. Only the velocity component perpendicular to $\mathbf r$ counts.
examples.review: Opus 5.5 wrote it from the confirmed note; Fable 5.1 solved it blind and checked the steps; code recomputed the answer (2026-09-23)

examples.problem: A uniform stick of mass $M=2.0$ kg and length $\ell=1.5$ m lies in the $x$-$y$ plane, pivoted at one end at the origin. It spins about the $z$ axis at $\omega=4.0$ rad/s. Find $L_z$.

steps.do: Put the stick along x from the pivot
steps.why: Then each piece is a distance $r=x$ from the $z$ axis.

steps.do: Integrate r² dm along the stick
steps.why: $I_z$ uses the distance from the rotation axis, here the pivot end.

steps.do: Evaluate the moment of inertia
steps.why: You need a number before multiplying by $\omega$.

steps.do: Multiply by ω to get L_z
steps.why: For a pancake spinning about $z$, $L_z=I_z\omega$ and $L_x=L_y=0$.

examples.takeaway: Find $I_z=\int r^2\,dm$ about the actual rotation axis, then $L_z=I_z\omega$.
examples.review: Opus 5.5 wrote it from the confirmed note; Fable 5.1 solved it blind and checked the steps; code recomputed the answer (2026-09-23)

examples.problem: A uniform stick has mass $m=2$ kg and length $\ell=1.5$ m. It rotates about a perpendicular axis through a point $\ell/6$ from one end. Find its moment of inertia about this axis.

steps.do: Start from the CM axis parallel to it
steps.why: The theorem only shifts from an axis through the CM, never between two axes that both miss the CM.

steps.do: Measure the distance from the CM to the axis
steps.why: $R$ is the perpendicular distance between the two parallel axes, measured from the CM, not from the end.

steps.do: Find the shift term
steps.why: All of the mass acts as if it sits at the CM, a distance $R$ from the new axis.

steps.do: Add the shift to I^CM
steps.why: $I$ always grows as the axis moves away from the CM, so you add $mR^2$ and never subtract it.

examples.takeaway: Always shift from the CM: $I=I^{\rm CM}+MR^2$, where $R$ is the distance from the CM axis.
examples.review: Opus 5.5 wrote it from the confirmed note; Fable 5.1 solved it blind and checked the steps; code recomputed the answer (2026-09-23)

examples.problem: A solid cylinder ($I=\tfrac12mr^2$) has mass $m=2$ kg and radius $r=0.1$ m. It rolls without slipping with CM speed $V=3$ m/s. Find its total kinetic energy.

steps.do: Split T into CM and spin parts
steps.why: About the CM the cross terms vanish, so the kinetic energy splits cleanly into two terms (Theorem 8.2).

steps.do: Get the spin rate from rolling
steps.why: Rolling without slipping ties the spin rate to the CM speed through $V=\omega r$.

steps.do: Compute the translational term
steps.why: This is the kinetic energy of the whole mass moving with the CM.

steps.do: Compute the rotational term about the CM
steps.why: Use $I$ about the CM here. Using $I$ about the contact point would count the translation twice.

steps.do: Add the two parts
steps.why: The total is the translational part plus the rotation about the CM.

examples.takeaway: $T=\tfrac12MV^2+\tfrac12I^{\rm CM}\omega'^2$: move the CM as a point mass, then add the spin about the CM.
examples.review: Opus 5.5 wrote it from the confirmed note; Fable 5.1 solved it blind and checked the steps; code recomputed the answer (2026-09-23)

examples.problem: A force $\mathbf F=(3,4)$ N acts at the point $\mathbf r=(2,1)$ m in the $xy$-plane. Find the torque about the origin, including its direction.

steps.do: Read off r from the origin, and F
steps.why: $\mathbf r$ must run from the chosen origin to the point where the force acts.

steps.do: Write the z-component of r × F
steps.why: For planar $\mathbf r$ and $\mathbf F$, the torque $\mathbf r\times\mathbf F$ points only along $z$.

steps.do: Plug in, keeping the order r × F
steps.why: Writing $\mathbf F\times\mathbf r$ instead would flip the sign, and so the direction.

steps.do: Turn the sign into a direction
steps.why: A positive $\tau_z$ means counterclockwise when viewed from $+z$, by the right-hand rule.

examples.takeaway: Torque is $\mathbf r\times\mathbf F$ from a stated origin; in the plane, $\tau_z=xF_y-yF_x$, and positive means counterclockwise.
examples.review: Opus 5.5 wrote it from the confirmed note; Fable 5.1 solved it blind and checked the steps; code recomputed the answer (2026-09-23)

examples.problem: A uniform solid cylinder ($I=\tfrac12MR^2$) rolls without slipping down a fixed incline at $\theta=30^\circ$. Use $\tau=dL/dt$ about the contact point, which is fixed on the plane, to find the acceleration of the CM.

steps.do: Choose the fixed contact point as origin
steps.why: A fixed point is a safe origin. Friction and the normal force act there, so they give no torque.

steps.do: Find the torque from gravity at the CM
steps.why: Only the component of gravity along the incline has a lever arm $R$ about the contact point.

steps.do: Write L, including the CM term
steps.why: About a fixed point, add the angular momentum of the CM as a point mass to the spin term.

steps.do: Set τ = dL/dt and solve
steps.why: Use the same origin for both the torque and $L$. The factors $M$ and $R$ cancel.

steps.do: Plug in the numbers

examples.takeaway: Take $\tau=dL/dt$ only about a fixed point or the CM; about a fixed point, include the $MvR$ term in $L$.
examples.review: Opus 5.5 wrote it from the confirmed note; Fable 5.1 solved it blind and checked the steps; code recomputed the answer (2026-09-23)

examples.problem: A uniform stick ($m=2$ kg, $\ell=1.2$ m) lies at rest on frictionless ice. A hammer gives it an impulse $J=3$ N·s at one end, perpendicular to the stick. Find the angular velocity just after the blow.

steps.do: Use the CM as origin
steps.why: The stick is free, so the CM is a legal origin. Don't use $I^{\rm end}=\tfrac13m\ell^2$.

steps.do: Find the lever arm of the blow
steps.why: $d$ is the perpendicular distance from the CM to the line of the blow.

steps.do: Set the angular impulse equal to ΔL
steps.why: $\Delta L=R\times\Delta p$. You never need the force profile $F(t)$.

steps.do: Solve for ω
steps.why: For comparison, the CM also moves off at $V=J/m=1.5$ m/s.

examples.takeaway: For a blow on a free body, $\Delta V_{CM}=J/M$ and $\Delta\omega=Jd/I_{CM}$, with $d$ measured from the CM.
examples.review: Opus 5.5 wrote it from the confirmed note; Fable 5.1 solved it blind and checked the steps; code recomputed the answer (2026-09-23)

examples.problem: A rigid disk's center $P$ moves at $\mathbf V_P=3\hat{\mathbf x}$ m/s. The disk rotates with $\boldsymbol\omega=8\hat{\mathbf z}$ rad/s about an axis through $P$. Point $Q$ of the disk sits at $\mathbf r-\mathbf r_P=0.5\hat{\mathbf x}$ m. Find $Q$'s speed in the lab frame.

steps.do: Take the center P as reference point
steps.why: Chasles: any rigid motion is $P$'s translation plus a rotation about an axis through $P$.

steps.do: Write Q's displacement from P
steps.why: The rotation acts on the position measured from $P$, not from the lab origin.

steps.do: Cross ω into the displacement, ω first
steps.why: $\hat{\mathbf z}\times\hat{\mathbf x}=\hat{\mathbf y}$. Writing $\mathbf r\times\boldsymbol\omega$ would flip the sign.

steps.do: Add P's translation velocity
steps.why: The lab velocity is $\mathbf V_P$ plus the rotation about $P$.

steps.do: Take the magnitude
steps.why: The two pieces are perpendicular. Check: the rotational part is $\omega r'=8(0.5)=4$ m/s.

examples.takeaway: Velocity of any body point: $\mathbf v=\mathbf V_P+\boldsymbol\omega\times(\mathbf r-\mathbf r_P)$, with $\boldsymbol\omega$ first.
examples.review: Opus 5.5 wrote it from the confirmed note; Fable 5.1 solved it blind and checked the steps; code recomputed the answer (2026-09-23)

examples.problem: A rigid body's reference point $P$ moves at $\mathbf V_P=2\hat{\mathbf x}$ m/s. The body rotates about an axis through $P$ with $\boldsymbol\omega=\omega_2\hat{\mathbf y}+\omega_3\hat{\mathbf z}$, where $\omega_2=2$ rad/s and $\omega_3=3$ rad/s. Point $Q$ sits at $\mathbf r-\mathbf r_P=x\hat{\mathbf x}$ with $x=0.5$ m. Find $Q$'s speed.

steps.do: Write ω and Q's position relative to P
steps.why: The components $(\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3)$ go into Eq. 9.6 in that order.

steps.do: Apply Eq. 9.6 with ω first
steps.why: Order matters: $\mathbf r\times\boldsymbol\omega$ would reverse the velocity.

steps.do: Add the reference point's velocity
steps.why: $P$ is moving, so $\boldsymbol\omega\times(\mathbf r-\mathbf r_P)$ alone gives only the velocity relative to $P$.

steps.do: Take the magnitude
steps.why: The speed is the length of the full velocity vector.

steps.do: Check the rotational part equals ω r′
steps.why: $Q$'s displacement is perpendicular to $\boldsymbol\omega$, so $r'=0.5$ m.

examples.takeaway: Write $\boldsymbol\omega$ with the right-hand rule, compute $\boldsymbol\omega\times(\mathbf r-\mathbf r_P)$ in components, then add $\mathbf V_P$.
examples.review: Opus 5.5 wrote it from the confirmed note; Fable 5.1 solved it blind and checked the steps; code recomputed the answer (2026-09-23)

examples.problem: A rigid body pivots about a fixed point at the origin. The body point $C$ at $(0,3,4)$ m is momentarily at rest. Point $Q$ at $(2,0,0)$ m moves with $\mathbf v_Q=(0,8,-6)$ m/s. Find $\boldsymbol\omega$.

steps.do: Put the origin at the pivot
steps.why: The pivot is on the axis, so every point obeys Eq. 9.1 measured from it.

steps.do: Draw the axis through the pivot and C
steps.why: $\mathbf v_C=0$ means $\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r_C=0$, so $\boldsymbol\omega\parallel\mathbf r_C$.

steps.do: Find Q's perpendicular distance to the axis
steps.why: The speed depends on the distance from the axis, not from the origin.

steps.do: Get the magnitude from Q's speed
steps.why: The two points at rest fix only the line. A third point's speed gives $\omega$.

steps.do: Fix the sign with the right-hand rule
steps.why: The plus sign reproduces $\mathbf v_Q$, so $\boldsymbol\omega$ points along $+\mathbf r_C$.

examples.takeaway: Two points at rest fix the line of $\boldsymbol\omega$. One moving point fixes its size and sign.
examples.review: Opus 5.5 wrote it from the confirmed note; Fable 5.1 solved it blind and checked the steps; code recomputed the answer (2026-09-23)

examples.problem: A sphere with a fixed center spins at $\omega_3=3$ rad/s about a stick along $\hat{\mathbf z}$, relative to the stick. The stick is turned about $\hat{\mathbf y}$ at $\omega_2=4$ rad/s. Find the sphere's lab-frame angular velocity and its magnitude at this instant.

steps.do: Name the frames: sphere, stick, lab
steps.why: Thm 9.3 chains rotations of nested frames that share an origin.

steps.do: Write the spin relative to the stick
steps.why: Right-hand rule along the stick. This vector is fixed in $S_2$.

steps.do: Write the stick's rotation relative to lab
steps.why: The stick turns about $\hat{\mathbf y}$ as seen in the lab.

steps.do: Add the two as vectors
steps.why: Linear velocities add, so angular velocities add: $\boldsymbol\omega_{1,3}=\boldsymbol\omega_{1,2}+\boldsymbol\omega_{2,3}$.

steps.do: Take the magnitude
steps.why: The pieces are perpendicular. Adding the scalars (7) would be wrong. Over time, $\boldsymbol\omega$ traces a cone about $y$.

examples.takeaway: Spin relative to the frame plus the frame's rotation, added as vectors: $\boldsymbol\omega_{1,3}=\boldsymbol\omega_{1,2}+\boldsymbol\omega_{2,3}$.
examples.review: Opus 5.5 wrote it from the confirmed note; Fable 5.1 solved it blind and checked the steps; code recomputed the answer (2026-09-23)

examples.problem: A wheel of radius $r=0.5$ m sits on a horizontal axle. The axle is pivoted at a fixed point $R=2$ m from the wheel's center. The axle turns about the vertical at $\Omega=3$ rad/s, and the wheel rolls without slipping. Find the spin $\omega'$ relative to the axle frame.

steps.do: Find the points at rest
steps.why: Points at rest lie on the axis of $\boldsymbol\omega$, so no slip is a condition on the contact point.

steps.do: Find the contact point's speed from precession
steps.why: The contact point is a horizontal distance $R$ from the vertical precession axis.

steps.do: Find its speed from spin relative to axle
steps.why: The contact point is on the rim, a distance $r$ from the wheel's axle.

steps.do: Make the two cancel (no slip)
steps.why: The total velocity of the contact point must vanish.

steps.do: Check the total ω lies along pivot–contact
steps.why: Theorem 9.3 sum. It points from the contact point up through the pivot, as it should.

examples.takeaway: No slip: the contact point's spin speed $\omega' r$ cancels its precession speed $\Omega R$, so $\omega'=(R/r)\Omega$.
examples.review: Opus 5.5 wrote it from the confirmed note; Fable 5.1 solved it blind and checked the steps; code recomputed the answer (2026-09-23)

examples.problem: A square of mass $m=2$ kg and side $a=0.5$ m, with one corner at the origin, has $\mathbf I=ma^2\begin{pmatrix}1/3&-1/4&0\\-1/4&1/3&0\\0&0&2/3\end{pmatrix}$. It rotates with $\boldsymbol\omega=(3,1,2)$ rad/s. Is $\mathbf I$ symmetric? Find $L_x$ of $\mathbf L=\mathbf I\boldsymbol\omega$.

steps.do: Compare mirror entries across the diagonal
steps.why: All pairs match, so $I_{ij}=I_{ji}$ and $\mathbf I$ is symmetric, as every inertia tensor is.

steps.do: Compute the prefactor $ma^2$
steps.why: Pull out the common factor so the matrix entries are pure numbers.

steps.do: Dot row $x$ into $\boldsymbol\omega$
steps.why: $L_x$ is row $x$ times $\omega_x,\omega_y,\omega_z$ in order. Keep the minus sign.

steps.do: Multiply by the prefactor
steps.why: The units are (units of $\mathbf I$) times (units of $\boldsymbol\omega$).

examples.takeaway: Each component of $\mathbf I\mathbf u$ is one row of $\mathbf I$ dotted into $\mathbf u$. The matrix is symmetric when $I_{ij}=I_{ji}$.
examples.review: Opus 5.5 wrote it from the confirmed note; Fable 5.1 solved it blind and checked the steps; code recomputed the answer (2026-09-23)

examples.problem: A uniform solid cube (mass $M$, side $L$) has its origin at a corner and axes along the edges, so $\mathbf I=ML^2\begin{pmatrix}2/3&-1/4&-1/4\\-1/4&2/3&-1/4\\-1/4&-1/4&2/3\end{pmatrix}$. It spins with $\boldsymbol\omega=\omega\hat{\mathbf z}$ about the $z$ edge. Find $\mathbf L$ and its angle from $\hat{\mathbf z}$.

steps.do: Put the origin on the axis, at the corner
steps.why: $\mathbf L=\mathbf I\boldsymbol\omega$ needs the origin on the rotation axis and orthonormal axes.

steps.do: Multiply the tensor by $\boldsymbol\omega$
steps.why: Only $\omega_3$ is nonzero, so $\mathbf L$ is the third column of $\mathbf I$ times $\omega$.

steps.do: Notice the nonzero $L_x$ and $L_y$
steps.why: The products of inertia are nonzero because the mass is off-center, so $\mathbf L\not\parallel\boldsymbol\omega$.

steps.do: Find the angle from $\cos\theta=L_z/|\mathbf L|$
steps.why: $\boldsymbol\omega\cdot\mathbf L/(\omega|\mathbf L|)$ reduces to $L_z/|\mathbf L|$ when $\boldsymbol\omega$ is along $z$.

steps.do: Take the arccosine
steps.why: This is the tilt of $\mathbf L$ away from the spin axis.

examples.takeaway: $\mathbf L=\mathbf I\boldsymbol\omega$ picks up the off-diagonal entries, so $\mathbf L$ tilts away from $\boldsymbol\omega$ unless the products of inertia vanish.
examples.review: Opus 5.5 wrote it from the confirmed note; Fable 5.1 solved it blind and checked the steps; code recomputed the answer (2026-09-23)

examples.problem: A uniform disk ($M=2$ kg, radius $b=0.1$ m) lies in the $x$-$y$ plane. Its CM is at $\mathbf R=(3,0,0)$ m and moves with $\mathbf V=(0,4,0)$ m/s. It spins with $\boldsymbol\omega=(0,0,10)$ rad/s about its symmetry axis. Find $L_z$ about the origin.

steps.do: Split the motion into the CM part plus spin
steps.why: The cross terms vanish because $\int\mathbf r'\,dm=0$ about the CM.

steps.do: Compute the orbital part $M\mathbf R\times\mathbf V$
steps.why: Treat the disk as a point mass $M$ at the CM. Keep the order $\mathbf R\times\mathbf V$.

steps.do: Find $\mathbf I_{\rm CM}$ about the disk's axis
steps.why: The CM axes are parallel to the fixed axes. A flat disk has $z'=0$, so $I_{xz}=I_{yz}=0$.

steps.do: Compute the spin part
steps.why: The spin angular momentum about the CM uses the body's $\boldsymbol\omega$.

steps.do: Add the components
steps.why: The total is the vector sum of the orbital and spin parts.

examples.takeaway: $\mathbf L$ about any origin is a point mass $M$ at the CM ($M\mathbf R\times\mathbf V$) plus the spin $\mathbf I_{\rm CM}\boldsymbol\omega$.

steps.why: A direct calculation of the speed confirms the tensor result.

steps.why: $\mathbf I_R$ is the point-mass tensor, so the minus sign appears just as in $-\int xy\,dm$.

steps.why: $\mathbf I=\mathbf I_R+\mathbf I_{\rm CM}$. The shift creates off-diagonal entries even though $\mathbf I_{\rm CM}$ is diagonal.

examples.problem: Find the eigenvalues and normalized eigenvectors of the symmetric matrix $A=\begin{pmatrix}5&2\\2&2\end{pmatrix}$.

steps.do: Subtract $\lambda$ from the diagonal entries only
steps.why: $A\mathbf u=\lambda\mathbf u$ is the same as $(A-\lambda\mathbf 1)\mathbf u=0$.

steps.do: Set the determinant to zero
steps.why: A nonzero $\mathbf u$ exists only if $\det(A-\lambda\mathbf 1)=0$.

steps.do: Solve the quadratic for $\lambda$
steps.why: The quadratic factors as $(\lambda-6)(\lambda-1)=0$. For a symmetric matrix the roots are real.

steps.do: Put $\lambda=6$ into the first row
steps.why: The second row gives the same condition, and $\det=0$ guarantees this redundancy. Normalize at the end.

steps.do: Put $\lambda=1$ into the first row
steps.why: Each eigenvector is fixed only up to a constant, so choose unit length.

steps.do: Check orthogonality, the trace and the determinant
steps.why: Symmetric matrices have orthogonal eigenvectors. The eigenvalues sum to the trace and multiply to the determinant.

examples.takeaway: Solve $\det(A-\lambda\mathbf 1)=0$, put each root back into one row to get the ratio of components, then normalize and check that the eigenvectors are orthogonal.

examples.problem: About its pivot, a body has inertia tensor (in kg·m²) $\mathbf I=\begin{pmatrix}5&2&0\\2&5&0\\0&0&3\end{pmatrix}$. Is $\hat{\boldsymbol\omega}=(1,1,0)/\sqrt2$ a principal axis? If the body spins at $\omega=2$ rad/s about this axis, find $|\mathbf L|$.

steps.do: Apply the tensor to the candidate axis
steps.why: A principal axis is one where $\mathbf I\hat{\boldsymbol\omega}$ comes out parallel to $\hat{\boldsymbol\omega}$.

steps.do: Compare the result with the axis
steps.why: It is an eigenvector, so the axis is principal. The eigenvalue is the principal moment.

steps.do: Read off the principal moment
steps.why: The eigenvalue $\lambda$ in $\mathbf I\boldsymbol\omega=\lambda\boldsymbol\omega$ is the moment about this axis.

steps.do: Multiply by ω to get L
steps.why: Along a principal axis, $\mathbf L\parallel\boldsymbol\omega$, so one scalar moment is enough.

examples.takeaway: To test an axis, apply $\mathbf I$ to it. If you get a multiple of the axis, it is principal, the multiple is $I$, and $\mathbf L=I\boldsymbol\omega$.

steps.why: $\hat{\mathbf e}_2$ is $120^\circ$ from $\hat{\mathbf x}$, and $\cos120^\circ$ is negative, so the minus sign is real.

steps.do: Check that the length is unchanged

examples.problem: A uniform disk ($M=2$ kg, $R=0.5$ m) spins at $\omega_s=10$ rad/s about its horizontal axle $\hat{\boldsymbol\omega}_3$. The axle turns at $\Omega=2$ rad/s about the vertical $\hat{\mathbf z}$, which lies along a diameter of the disk. Find $|\mathbf L|$ about the CM.

steps.why: A disk has rotational symmetry about its axle, so every diameter is also principal.

steps.do: Multiply component by component
steps.why: The inertia tensor is diagonal in the principal basis: $L_i=I_i\omega_i$.

examples.problem: A flat plate has inertia tensor about its pivot, in units of $ma^2$, $\mathbf I=\begin{pmatrix}5&2&0\\2&2&0\\0&0&7\end{pmatrix}$. Find the principal moments and principal axes.

steps.do: Spot any axis that is already principal
steps.why: With zeros in its row and column, only the $2\times2$ block is left to diagonalize.

steps.do: Set the block determinant to zero
steps.why: $(\mathbf I-\lambda\mathbf 1)\mathbf v=0$ has a nonzero solution only if the determinant vanishes.

steps.do: Solve for the roots
steps.why: The roots are the in-plane principal moments, in units of $ma^2$.

steps.do: Find the eigenvector for λ = 6
steps.why: Substitute the root back into $(\mathbf I-\lambda\mathbf 1)\mathbf v=0$, then normalize.

steps.do: Find the eigenvector for λ = 1
steps.why: This must be orthogonal to $\hat{\boldsymbol\omega}_1$. Check: $2-2=0$.

steps.do: Check against the trace
steps.why: The sum of the principal moments must equal $\mathrm{tr}\,\mathbf I$.

examples.problem: A uniform square plate ($M=2$ kg, side $a=0.5$ m) is pivoted at a corner. It rotates at $\omega=4$ rad/s about one of its sides. About the corner, the principal moments are $Ma^2/12$ (diagonal), $7Ma^2/12$ (in-plane, perpendicular to the diagonal) and $2Ma^2/3$ ($z$). Find the kinetic energy.

steps.why: About the corner, the sides are not symmetry axes, so the product of inertia does not cancel.

steps.do: Name the principal axes by symmetry
steps.why: The diagonal is a mirror line through the corner, so $\int$(product)$\,dm$ cancels in pairs.

steps.why: $\hat{\mathbf x}$ is $45^\circ$ from both in-plane principal axes.

steps.do: Sum the principal-axis energies
steps.why: In the principal basis, $T=\tfrac12\sum I_k\omega_k^2$ with no cross terms.

steps.do: Plug in the numbers
steps.why: Check: this equals $\tfrac12(Ma^2/3)\omega^2$, using the moment about a side.

examples.problem: A free rectangular block has principal moments $I_1=0.005$, $I_2=0.004$, $I_3=0.002$ kg m$^2$. It spins at $\omega_2=10$ rad/s about the intermediate axis 2 with a tiny wobble. Find the exponential growth rate of the small components $\omega_1$ and $\omega_3$.

steps.why: The body is free, with the origin at the CM. Each $\omega_i$ is measured along a principal axis.

steps.do: Treat $\omega_2$ as large, $\omega_1,\omega_3$ as small
steps.why: The right side is a product of two small quantities, so drop it to first order.

steps.do: Combine the $\omega_1$ and $\omega_3$ equations
steps.why: This is the linearized equation with spin axis $a=2$, obtained by cyclic relabeling.

steps.do: Evaluate the coefficient $K$
steps.why: $K<0$ because $I_2$ is the intermediate moment. The solutions are exponentials, not oscillations.

steps.do: Take the growth rate $\lambda=\sqrt{-K}$
steps.why: Since $\omega_1\propto e^{\lambda t}$, the wobble grows and spin about axis 2 is unstable.

examples.problem: Model the earth as a torque-free symmetric top with $(I_3-I)/I=1/320$. It spins at $\omega_3=2\pi$ rad/day, and $\boldsymbol\omega$ is tilted slightly from $\hat{\mathbf x}_3$. Seen from the earth, what is the period of the precession of $\boldsymbol\omega$ about $\hat{\mathbf x}_3$?

steps.do: Set $I_1=I_2=I$ and all $\tau_i=0$
steps.why: These are Euler's equations for a free symmetric top about its CM.

steps.do: Use the third equation for $\omega_3$
steps.why: A constant $\omega_3$ makes the precession rate $\Omega$ constant.

steps.do: Define $\Omega$ and solve the transverse equations
steps.why: $\dot\omega_1=-\Omega\omega_2$ and $\dot\omega_2=\Omega\omega_1$ mean the transverse part moves in a circle at rate $\Omega$.

steps.do: Insert the earth's numbers
steps.why: Only $(I_3-I)/I$ and $\omega_3$ matter. The tilt size $A$ does not enter.

steps.do: Convert the rate to a period
steps.why: The observed Chandler wobble is about 430 days because the real earth is not rigid.

examples.problem: A thrown plate (disk) has $I=0.01$ kg m$^2$ and $I_3=0.02$ kg m$^2$ about its CM. It spins with $\omega_3=12$ rad/s and has transverse part $A=10$ rad/s. Seen from the ground, how fast does its symmetry axis precess around $\mathbf L$?

steps.why: $I$ is the transverse moment, and $A=\sqrt{\omega_1^2+\omega_2^2}$.

steps.do: Compute the conserved $L$
steps.why: With no torque, $\mathbf L$ is fixed in space. It is the axis of the precession.

steps.do: Divide $L$ by the transverse moment $I$
steps.why: $\dot{\hat{\mathbf x}}_3=(\frac{L}{I}\hat{\mathbf L})\times\hat{\mathbf x}_3$, because the $\Omega\hat{\mathbf x}_3$ part of $\boldsymbol\omega$ drops out.

steps.do: Compare with the body-frame rate
steps.why: The two frames give different rates. They agree through $\boldsymbol\omega=\frac{L}{I}\hat{\mathbf L}-\Omega\hat{\mathbf x}_3$.

examples.takeaway: In the fixed frame, $\hat{\mathbf x}_3$ and $\boldsymbol\omega$ precess around the fixed $\mathbf L$ at $L/I$, with the transverse moment $I$ in the denominator.

steps.do: Name the angles and their rates
steps.why: $\theta$ is the tilt from $\hat{\mathbf z}$, $\phi$ is the precession about $\hat{\mathbf z}$, and $\psi$ is the spin about $\hat{\mathbf x}_3$.

steps.do: Add the rotations as vectors
steps.why: Angular velocities add as vectors, and $\dot\theta=0$ removes the $\hat{\mathbf x}_1$ term.

steps.do: Project $\hat{\mathbf z}$ onto the orthogonal axes
steps.why: $\hat{\mathbf z}$ and $\hat{\mathbf x}_3$ are not orthogonal, so we need orthogonal components first.

steps.do: Collect the components
steps.why: $\omega_3=\dot\psi+\dot\phi\cos\theta$, not just $\dot\psi$.

steps.do: Take the magnitude
steps.why: Pythagoras only works on orthogonal components.

steps.why: The vertical part stays constant. The horizontal parts of $\mathbf L_3$ and $\mathbf L_2$ point in opposite directions.

steps.do: Set Ω L_⊥ equal to gravity's torque

steps.do: Factor out the leading piece
steps.why: Now the correction has the form $(1+x)^n$ with $x=-\theta^2/2$ and $n=-1/2$.

steps.why: $nx=(-\tfrac12)(-\tfrac{\theta^2}{2})=+\theta^2/4$. Watch the signs.

steps.do: Check the θ → 0 limit
steps.why: At zero angle it reduces to the simple-pendulum result, as it should.

examples.problem: A top has $M=0.2$ kg and $\ell=0.04$ m. Its moment about a horizontal axis through the pivot is $I=5\times10^{-4}$ kg·m², and its moment about the symmetry axis is $I_3=2\times10^{-4}$ kg·m². Take $g=9.8$ m/s². What is the minimum spin $\omega_3$ for it to sleep stably upright?

steps.do: Fix L_z by the vertical start
steps.why: The top starts at $\theta=0$, so $L_z=I_3\omega_3$ for all later times.

steps.do: Expand for small θ to get φ̇
steps.why: $\sin^2\theta\approx\theta^2$ and $1-\cos\theta\approx\theta^2/2$. This $\dot\phi$ is not small.

steps.do: Substitute into the exact θ equation
steps.why: Keep the $I\dot\phi^2\cos\theta$ term. It supplies half of the $\omega_3^2$ coefficient.

steps.do: Require a positive coefficient
steps.why: A positive coefficient gives oscillation, so $\theta$ stays small. A negative one makes $\theta$ grow exponentially.

steps.do: Plug in the numbers
steps.why: $IMg\ell=5\times10^{-4}\cdot0.0784$ J·kg·m².

examples.takeaway: Fix $L_z=I_3\omega_3$, which forces $\dot\phi=I_3\omega_3/2I$. Keep every term in the $\theta$ equation, then require $I_3^2\omega_3^2>4IMg\ell$.

examples.problem: Morin's triangle floats freely. It has $m=1$ kg at $A$ and at $B$, and $2m$ at the right-angle vertex $C$. The hypotenuse is $4a$, with $a=0.5$ m. With the CM at the origin, $\mathbf r_B=(2a,-a,0)$. $B$ gets an impulse $P=2$ N·s into the page. Find $|\boldsymbol\omega|$ just after the blow.

steps.do: Put the origin at the CM; write r and P
steps.why: For a free body, measure from the CM. Into the page is $-z$.

steps.do: Take the cross product r × P
steps.why: The blow is so quick that $\mathbf r$ stays fixed, so $\mathbf L=\int\boldsymbol\tau\,dt=\mathbf r\times\mathbf P$.

steps.do: Find the principal moments about the CM
steps.why: Mirror symmetry about the $y$ axis makes $x,y,z$ principal. For a flat body, $I_z=I_x+I_y$.

steps.do: Solve I_k ω_k = L_k one component at a time
steps.why: Each component has its own $I_k$. So $\boldsymbol\omega\propto(1,1,0)$ even though $\mathbf L\propto(1,2,0)$.

steps.do: Take the magnitude and plug in the numbers
steps.why: The vector $(1,1,0)$ has length $\sqrt2$.

examples.takeaway: Get $\mathbf L=\mathbf r\times\mathbf P$ from the blow, then divide each component by its own principal moment; $\boldsymbol\omega$ need not be parallel to $\mathbf L$.

examples.problem: A rigid rod of length $A=2$ m points out from a fixed pivot at angle $\theta=\pi/3$ to a vertical axis. It turns about that axis at $\Omega=3$ rad/s. Find the speed of its tip, $|d\vec A/dt|$.

steps.do: Point Ω along the rotation axis
steps.why: By the right-hand rule, $\vec\Omega$ lies along the axis, and its size is the turning rate.

steps.do: Split A into parts along and across the axis
steps.why: Only $\vec A_\perp$ moves. The part along the axis stays fixed.

steps.do: Use dA/dt = Ω × A
steps.why: The tip moves on a circle of radius $A\sin\theta$, at rate $\Omega$.

steps.do: Plug in the numbers
steps.why: $\sin(\pi/3)=\sqrt3/2$. Use $\sin\theta$, not the full length $A$.

examples.takeaway: For a fixed-length vector turning about $\vec\Omega$, $d\vec A/dt=\vec\Omega\times\vec A$, and only $\vec A_\perp$ moves: the speed is $\Omega A\sin\theta$.

examples.problem: A uniform stick of length $\ell=0.6$ m is pivoted at its top end. It swings around the vertical axis at a constant $\theta=60^\circ$ from the vertical. Find its angular frequency $\omega$. Use $g=9.8$ m/s².

steps.do: Put the origin at the pivot
steps.why: The unknown pivot force then gives no torque. $y$ is along the stick.

steps.do: Write L in principal axes
steps.why: $\boldsymbol\omega=(\omega\sin\theta,\omega\cos\theta,0)$ and $I_y=0$, so $\mathbf L$ is perpendicular to the stick, not vertical.

steps.do: Rotate only the horizontal part of L
steps.why: $d\mathbf L/dt=\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf L$. The vertical part of $\mathbf L$ does not change.

steps.do: Find gravity's torque, acting at the CM
steps.why: The CM is at $\ell/2$ from the pivot. The torque points into the page, the same way as $d\mathbf L/dt$.

steps.do: Set τ equal to |dL/dt| and solve
steps.why: The factors $m$ and $\sin\theta$ cancel from both sides.

examples.takeaway: Take torques about the pivot, and set $\tau$ equal to $\omega$ times the part of $\mathbf L$ perpendicular to $\boldsymbol\omega$.

examples.problem: A torque-free symmetric body has $I_1=I_2=I=2$ kg·m² and $I_3=3$ kg·m². It spins with $\omega_3=4$ rad/s plus a small wobble. Seen from the body, at what rate $\Omega$ does $\boldsymbol\omega$ circle the $\hat{\mathbf x}_3$ axis?

steps.do: Write Euler's equations with zero torque
steps.why: No torque means $\tau_i=0$. The axes are principal and fixed in the body, with the origin at the CM.

steps.do: Use I_1 = I_2 in the third equation
steps.why: The symmetry makes the $\omega\omega$ term vanish.

steps.do: Rewrite the first two equations with Ω
steps.why: Dividing by $I$ puts both equations in the same form.

steps.do: Differentiate once to get SHM
steps.why: $(\omega_1,\omega_2)$ goes around a circle at frequency $\Omega$.

steps.do: Plug in the numbers
steps.why: $I_3>I$, so the motion is counterclockwise, looking down from $+\hat{\mathbf x}_3$.

examples.takeaway: In principal body axes, use $\tau_1=I_1\dot\omega_1+(I_3-I_2)\omega_3\omega_2$ and its cyclic versions. For a free symmetric top, $\boldsymbol\omega$ circles $\hat{\mathbf x}_3$ at $\Omega=(I_3-I)\omega_3/I$.

examples.problem: A $0.5$ kg mass on a spring with $k=200$ N/m is pulled to $x_0=0.1$ m and released from rest at $t=0$. Find its position at $t=0.1$ s.

steps.do: Write F = ma
steps.why: A linear restoring force, with $x$ measured from equilibrium.

steps.do: Divide by the coefficient of ẍ
steps.why: $\ddot x$ must have coefficient 1 before you read off $\omega^2$.

steps.do: Read off ω
steps.why: The factor multiplying $-x$ is $\omega^2=k/m$.

steps.do: Fix the constants from the initial conditions
steps.why: A second-order equation needs both $x_0$ and $v_0$.

steps.do: Evaluate in radians
steps.why: $\omega t=2$ is in radians, not degrees.

examples.takeaway: Divide until $\ddot x$ stands alone. Whatever multiplies $-x$ is $\omega^2$, and then $x=C_1\cos\omega t+C_2\sin\omega t$.
